# Peripartum Cardiomyopathy: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is an idiopathic form of heart failure that presents toward the end of pregnancy or in the months following delivery, in the absence of another identifiable cause of cardiac dysfunction [1]. It is characterized by left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction, with an ejection fraction (EF) typically below 45% [2]. Although relatively uncommon, PPCM is an important cause of maternal morbidity and mortality worldwide and remains underrecognized in many clinical settings [3].

## Epidemiology

The incidence of PPCM varies markedly by geographic region, reflecting differences in genetic background, socioeconomic factors, and diagnostic awareness [4]. Reported rates range from approximately 1 in 1,000 live births in South Africa to 1 in 1,000–4,000 in the United States, with strikingly high rates reported in Nigeria and Haiti [5]. Established risk factors include advanced maternal age, multiparity, multiple gestation, pre-eclampsia, hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, and African ancestry [6,7]. Registry data from the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) EORP program have provided contemporary insights into the global distribution and clinical features of the disease [8].

## Pathophysiology

The pathogenesis of PPCM is incompletely understood but is increasingly attributed to a "two-hit" model combining systemic vascular and hormonal stress with individual susceptibility [9]. A central mechanism involves oxidative stress in the late gestational period, which activates cathepsin D to cleave the nursing hormone prolactin into a 16-kDa antiangiogenic and proapoptotic fragment that damages the myocardial microvasculature [10]. The placentally derived antiangiogenic factor soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt-1) further contributes to endothelial and cardiac dysfunction, linking PPCM mechanistically to pre-eclampsia [11]. Genetic predisposition is also significant: truncating variants in *TTN* (encoding titin) are found in approximately 15% of patients, overlapping with the genetic architecture of dilated cardiomyopathy [12,13].

## Clinical Presentation and Diagnosis

The diagnosis of PPCM is one of exclusion and requires a high index of suspicion, as symptoms such as dyspnea, fatigue, and peripheral edema may be attributed to normal pregnancy [14]. Patients may present with overt heart failure, arrhythmias, or thromboembolic complications [15]. Echocardiography is the cornerstone of diagnosis, documenting reduced LVEF and frequently LV dilation [2]. Natriuretic peptides (BNP and NT-proBNP) are elevated and aid in distinguishing PPCM from physiologic dyspnea [16]. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging may help characterize myocardial tissue and exclude alternative etiologies, although gadolinium use is generally avoided during pregnancy [17].

## Management

Management of PPCM follows general heart failure principles, with important modifications for pregnancy and lactation [18]. In women who remain pregnant, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists are contraindicated due to fetotoxicity; beta-blockers (preferably beta-1 selective) and hydralazine with nitrates are preferred [19]. After delivery, guideline-directed medical therapy can be fully implemented [20]. Anticoagulation is recommended in patients with very low EF given the elevated thromboembolic risk associated with both PPCM and the peripartum state [21].

Bromocriptine, a dopamine agonist that blocks prolactin release, has emerged as a disease-specific therapy targeting the 16-kDa prolactin pathway [22]. A proof-of-concept trial and a subsequent multicenter study suggested improved LV recovery with bromocriptine added to standard therapy, although it must be accompanied by prophylactic anticoagulation [23,24]. Current ESC guidance supports its consideration, while emphasizing that evidence remains limited [25]. For refractory cases, mechanical circulatory support and cardiac transplantation may be required [26].

## Prognosis and Subsequent Pregnancies

Outcomes in PPCM are more favorable than in many other cardiomyopathies, with substantial myocardial recovery in 50–70% of patients, typically within 6–12 months [27]. Nonetheless, a subset develops persistent dysfunction, and mortality remains significant, particularly in low-resource settings [28]. Predictors of poor recovery include a markedly reduced baseline EF, larger LV dimensions, and non-white ethnicity [29]. Subsequent pregnancies carry meaningful risk of relapse, especially when LV function has not normalized, and require careful pre-conception counseling and multidisciplinary monitoring [30].

## Conclusion

PPCM is a distinct and potentially reversible cause of heart failure with a unique hormonal and genetic pathophysiology. Increased awareness, prompt diagnosis, evidence-based heart failure therapy, and emerging disease-specific treatments such as bromocriptine have improved outcomes. Continued research into mechanisms, biomarkers, and optimal management—particularly in high-incidence, resource-limited regions—remains a priority.
